title: Memorized repertoire and Duke's cues
summary: Two-thirds were memorised and Duke cued tunes by piano intros.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Now, when you had a repertoire this size, how did the guys -- did they memorize most of that music?

Two-thirds. Two thirds of it was memorized. Duke insisted on that. Because it mystified the average band, He wouldn't have to call 23 or 44 or different numbers, because when we started playing we would pay eight or 16 bars, just him and I and the bass. Anything. But when it got down near the last six bars, he would give them a tonic so the boys in the band would know what number we're playing. And he would turn around and give them that direct cue. So he would look at me and I would say to the guys, "we're rolling." That would make them ready. And after he played them bars, he would look up and man, that band would blast out there, that first one would kill you. (Laughter) Solid!---- would kill you.

That's how we -- and they never could understand. None of the bands'dn understand know what we were doing. Count does a little of it, you know. I noticed at the concert he would play not every number, but he would play a little--you know how Count Basie--tinkle it a little bit. And get up there and do like this and the band would shout. Well, he got that from Duke. Ain't no "one-two, one-two" you know, like Lawrence Welk or Woody Herman, all them bands.

Man, we played 16 bars and that was it. Sometimes just eight. The average guy wouldn't know what the hell he was playing until he'd give it to -- he'd say "watch it." And I'd turn around and holler back, "rolling". And that was it. And guys asked him a million times, how do you do that?

"I don't know." He'd shrug it off. But it was just a thing he picked up. I don't know where he picked it up from. But that's -- you never seen the one-two, one-two stomp off. If we stomp off when we're making a record. Because, I mean, in reality, stage or dance, that was it.
And we knew just what was happening.
So memorization was very, very important.
It was very important and it was necessary, you know.

Well, that also made it possible for some of those things like you were talking about, like for the band to start playing in the dark, too, without any -- sometimes you'd be playing and the spotlight might be on just one person.
Benny would be black, so you all weren't using those little music stands with the lights on them like they use today?
No. We had music stand but we didn't have a whole lot of lights strung out on them like they use. They knew what was happening. That's right. Something else.
